question: What is taraweeh, how did it begin, why is it called taraweeh, and is it 8 or 20 rak'ahs?
asked: What is Salat al-Taraweeh, where did it get its name from, and what is its relationship to qiyam al-layl?
answer:
So the concept of taraweeh and when it was introduced, and what is its relationship to the night prayer, or tahajjud, or qiyam al-layl? Realize that taraweeh is the name given to the qiyam al-layl, or to the salat al-tahajjud, during the nights of Ramadan. When we say tahajjud or when we say qiyam al-layl, this is the night prayer. And the night prayer is done anytime from salat al-'Isha up until before salat al-Fajr.

And the night prayer, or the qiyam al-layl, or the tahajjud, is one of the most blessed prayers after the fard prayer. And Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala commands our Prophet ﷺ in particular to pray the tahajjud prayer:

> وَمِنَ اللَّيْلِ فَتَهَجَّدْ بِهِ نَافِلَةً لَكَ عَسَىٰ أَنْ يَبْعَثَكَ رَبُّكَ مَقَامًا مَحْمُودًا

The maqam al-mahmud, the highest maqam, is linked to our Prophet ﷺ praying the night prayer. *Wa min al-layl*: and during the night, *fa-tahajjad bihi*: pray the tahajjud prayer. *Nafilatan lak*: it is a nafil, it's not a wajib. It is something that is supererogatory; it's not obligatory on you. By the way, some 'ulama did say that it was obligatory for our Prophet ﷺ only and not for the rest of us, and so when Allah is saying *nafilah*, He is not intending that for the Prophet ﷺ it is nafil. Some 'ulama said that it is wajib for our Prophet ﷺ only, because Allah says, *Qum al-layla illa qalila*: stand for the night except for a little bit of the night, when you sleep in.

The point being, taraweeh is tahajjud in Ramadan. Taraweeh is qiyam al-layl in Ramadan. When we do the nightly prayers in this blessed month, it is called taraweeh. And the concept of qiyam al-layl, or tahajjud, is something that we should all familiarize ourselves with, because all of the blessings of tahajjud apply to taraweeh as well.

And in one hadith our Prophet ﷺ said, and it is a hasan or authentic hadith, *'Alaykum bi-qiyam al-layl*: I command you to pray, or meaning I encourage you to pray, at night, *fa-innahu da'b al-salihin qablakum*, because it was the custom of the righteous peoples before you. So it was the custom, number one, of the righteous peoples before us. Number two, *wa qurbatun ila rabbikum*: and it is something that will bring you close to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala. Number three, *wa mukaffiratun lil-sayyi'at*: it forgives the evil deeds, it expiates the evil deeds. And number four, *wa manhatun 'an al-ithm*: and it prevents you from doing other sin. When you pray tahajjud, automatically it acts as a barrier from doing other evil deeds.

So four beautiful blessings are mentioned for salat al-tahajjud. Number one, it is the custom of the righteous before and after. You want to be from the elite, you want to be from the saliheen, you want to get an A in the eyes of Allah? Then it must come with salat al-tahajjud. Number two, it brings you close to Allah. Number three, it forgives your past sins. And number four, it is going to be a barrier between you and other sins.

And in the hadith in Tirmidhi, the famous hadith, our Prophet ﷺ described some beautiful places in Jannah that are so beautiful that the palaces are made out of glass, or they're made out of crystal, that you can see inside and outside. And they said, "Ya Rasulallah, who are those beautiful places, the highest, the ghuraf, meant for?" So the Prophet said: to those who do four things, who speak well all the time, they're not vulgar, they're not evil; and they give food to the hungry; and they fast; and they pray at night when people are asleep.

So this is some of the many, many blessings of qiyam al-layl. But in Ramadan, qiyam al-layl takes on the highest status. Why? Many reasons. Of them is the famous hadith that we all hear, and Ramadan is around the corner, so let's refresh ourselves with it. It is muttafaqun 'alayh, Bukhari and Muslim. Our Prophet ﷺ said that whoever fasts Ramadan *imanan wa ihtisaban*, all of his past sins are forgiven. And whoever stands the nights of Ramadan, *wa man qama Ramadan*, and the qiyam here means praying taraweeh, the qiyam here means praying tahajjud in the nights of Ramadan. So whoever prays in the nights of Ramadan extra prayer, that's taraweeh, whoever prays that qiyam, all of his previous sins are going to be forgiven.

Therefore, dear Muslims, taraweeh is no joke. Taraweeh guarantees, if you repent to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, a forgiveness of all of the previous sins that you have done. It is one of the main mechanisms to forgive all of our sins. So let us make it a niyyah from now, every one of us, that unless we have an excuse, we are sick, or our sisters, they might have that time of the month, other than that, let us make it the intention that every single night of this month that is going to come, without exception, we shall do some extra nafil, extra prayers that we typically don't do. And that is the name given to salat al-taraweeh.

Now, who instituted taraweeh? Where did it begin? It is narrated in the authentic books of hadith, in Sahih Bukhari and others, that our Prophet ﷺ, one night in the nights of taraweeh, prayed in the masjid on his own. There was no institutionalized taraweeh. He prayed on his own, and some people were also praying, and so when they saw him pray, they prayed behind him. It was not announced. It was not something that the call came out, the adhan was given. No, he happened to be praying tahajjud, qiyam al-layl. The people behind him saw him pray, and so they just decided to join.

News spread. The next day, more than double, it is said, the people came, so the masjid was very much full, and when the Prophet ﷺ came out and prayed the qiyam al-layl, the people behind him also prayed. Then on the third night the news spread across the whole city, and the masjid was jam-packed; the masjid was full of people. Then the Prophet ﷺ did not come, and the whole night went and he did not come. Then he came out at Fajr, and the masjid was still there, and he said to them, "I knew you were here. I wasn't sleeping, I was praying tahajjud. I knew you were here, but the only reason I did not come out and lead you was I was worried that it might become obligatory." I was worried that either Allah 'azza wa jall would make it obligatory, and then it would have been difficult for you, or some other people would assume that it's obligatory. So as a rahmah for you, as a mercy for you, I did not come out and pray.

And that was the last Ramadan of his life ﷺ, and he passed away. And therefore the concept, or the institution, of praying was just established. And then Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala caused him to come back to Himself. Then during the time of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq radiyallahu 'anhu, nothing happened. The people would just pray in the masjid on their own. During the first year of Umar's time as well, it is said that that would happen.

Perhaps in the second year, some say, in the time of Umar ibn al-Khattab radiyallahu 'anhu, it is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari from Abdur Rahman ibn Zayd al-Qari that he said: one night, myself and Umar ibn al-Khattab, we walked outside, and it was one of the nights of Ramadan, and we went to the Masjid of the Prophet ﷺ, and we saw groups of people praying on their own or in small jama'at. Somebody's praying on his own, somebody's praying with one imam, somebody's praying with a small group, and they're all in the masjid helter-skelter, split up. And so Umar ibn al-Khattab said, "I feel that we should combine all of these people upon one qari." And he then decided to choose Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who was one of the main qurra'. Our Prophet ﷺ said that whoever wants to learn the Qur'an, let him learn from one of four, and number one on the list was Ubayy ibn Ka'b. So Ubayy ibn Ka'b is considered to be the qari of the Sahabah, and many blessings are mentioned about Ubayy. I have a life story about Ubayy; you can listen to that online.

And then the next night Ubayy was leading, and the entire congregation was in one jama'ah, and Umar ibn al-Khattab was very happy, and he said, "*Ni'mat al-bid'atu hadhihi*," what a great new thing that we have done. And this is a deep theological controversy: what did he mean, etc. I've given another lecture about that. It's not something I like to do, to encourage you to listen to other lectures, but I don't have time to go to all of these other tangents. I have given an entire lecture about the reality of bid'ah, or innovation, between the various philosophies and schools out there, and so you can listen to that talk. And this narration of Umar ibn al-Khattab plays a very crucial role, because he said, "What a great bid'ah is this." What did he mean? How has it been interpreted? That is a different topic. But for now we understand what he is saying is that yesterday everybody was helter-skelter, today everybody is combined in one jama'ah: what a great thing that it is.

And then he said, "...*afdal min allati yaqumun*": those who are sleeping right now are better than those who are praying. And then the narrator himself said he meant those who will wake up at the end of the night are better than those who are praying it now. Now, we're going to come back to this point.

Now, this is the first year. Eventually, books of history mention to us that Umar ibn al-Khattab would appoint two imams for the men, and they would alternate back and forth. And then eventually, when the sisters could not hear, he appointed an imam for the sisters. Remember, there's no microphone, there's no loudspeaker, so the sisters are all in the back, they cannot hear, so he appointed another imam for them. And for the men he would also have alternating, either one day, one day, or, some say, some rak'at.

And when he instituted taraweeh, he instituted it upon what the Prophet ﷺ himself used to do. As Aisha says, he never prayed more than 11 rak'at a night. And so it was 8 rak'at of taraweeh and then 3 rak'at of witr; that is a total of 11. However, towards the end of his khilafah, after a few years, because Umar ibn al-Khattab was the khalifah for 10 solid years, remember, towards the end of his khilafah, some say in the middle of his khilafah, he changed 8 and he made it 20 rak'at, with witr to make it 23.

Why did he do this? The famous Maliki scholar al-Baji from Andalus, the great Maliki scholar al-Baji, said the wisdom why Umar ibn al-Khattab took it from 8 to 20 is to make it easier for the people, because the 8 rak'ahs would be so long that the people would bring their sticks and they would stand to get support. It would get so long. And so he made it 20 to make it easier for them: smaller bits, they can rest and whatnot.

And when he made it 20, they also began another habit, or a custom, that goes back to the Prophet ﷺ. What is this custom? Aisha says that the Prophet ﷺ would pray 4, then he would take a break, pray another 4, and she said, don't even ask how beautiful and long they were. Beautiful and long: that's the point of taraweeh. Then he would take a break, then pray another four, two, two, then take a break, then he would pray three rak'at witr.

So from this, in the time of Umar ibn al-Khattab, they derived a custom, or a habit, and that was after every four rak'at, two, two, after every four, they would take a break. And this break, or this rest, in Arabic has a word, and that is *tarwihah*. Tarwihah means an interlude; tarwihah means a break. And the plural of tarwihah is taraweeh. And so taraweeh means multiple interludes, or multiple resting breaks. That's the meaning of taraweeh, and this is why the taraweeh prayer was called taraweeh.

And the earliest person I could find, FYI, who said this was the famous Hanafi imam al-Sarakhsi in his *Kitab al-Mabsut*. He says that Imam Abu Hanifa explained why they called it taraweeh, and he mentions this point, that they would rest after every four rak'at. And Abu Hanifa rahimahullah passes away in the year 150 Hijrah, so he's talking about what he heard from his teachers, who are the Tabi' al-Tabi'in, and they are learning from the Tabi'in and the Sahabah. And so this notion of taraweeh being breaks after every four, this is something that goes back to this name, taraweeh.

Now, the people of Medina began praying this 20 rak'at. And why 20, by the way? It does not appear that there's any particular reason or wisdom why Umar ibn al-Khattab went to 20 rak'at. It's just a number that was more convenient. Perhaps he wanted to double to 16, then... I don't know, we're just assuming. Nobody knows why it was 20. But Umar ibn al-Khattab did institute the number 20.

And this custom then spread to Mecca. From Medina it started, obviously, because the caliphate was in Medina; Umar ibn al-Khattab lived in Medina. It then spread to Mecca, and within a few years, or a generation maybe, at the very max a generation, the people of Mecca would do something else. SubhanAllah, this is what happens when you are in Mecca: after every four rak'at, during that interlude, that break (you know, we said taraweeh means the tarwihah, or the breaks), after every four rak'at there would be that break, and so people began standing up and doing tawaf in that break, and then coming back to continue the taraweeh.

Now somebody can say, how can they possibly do tawaf in a break? And we respond: realize that when there is no rush and no crowd, it is very easy to do tawaf very quickly. And subhanAllah, I have done more umrah than I can count. I mean literally, may Allah accept, more than a thousand umrahs I have done in my life, and there have been times that I have done a tawaf in less than 11 minutes. I have timed myself. These days it's almost impossible to... well, right now it is empty; may Allah bring the crowds back, we miss those crowds. But when I would go and it would be crowded, I would miss my times when I used to go as a student, and I would go in the middle of the season and I would do it at 3 a.m. or something, and it was absolutely dead empty, and you could kiss the black stone, and you could do tawaf in 11 or 12 minutes, walking at a moderate pace.

So this is the taraweeh. Now, the people of Mecca regularly began doing tawaf after every four rak'at. SubhanAllah, when the people of Medina heard (we don't know exactly when, but estimate around 100 Hijrah, 120 Hijrah), so this is going back and forth, the people of Mecca and Medina are competing with one another for good. When the people of Medina heard this, they decided, because they cannot do tawaf, what should they do? They decided they're going to increase the number of rak'ahs of taraweeh. And so they decided to pray, instead of 20, a generation after Umar ibn al-Khattab, 36 rak'ahs. They added 16 rak'ahs, and then 3 to make it a total of 39, almost 40, like they wanted to almost double it. So 39 rak'ahs they would begin to pray, with witr.

And that's what we find Imam al-Shafi'i saying. The famous scholar al-Za'farani asked Imam al-Shafi'i, "What do you think about taraweeh?" Imam al-Shafi'i said: I saw the people of Medina praying 39 (we explained, 36 plus 3, 39; there was 36 of taraweeh), and I saw the people of Mecca praying 23 rak'ahs, and there is no harm in whichever position you want to follow.

And Imam al-Shafi'i also said that if they lengthen the qiyam and they make the sajdahs small, that is good. If they make the qiyam (the qiyam here means the recitation), if they recite very long surahs and they make the sajdahs short, that's good. And if they recite smaller surahs and they make the sajdahs long, that too is good. But I prefer the first. I prefer for taraweeh that the recitation is long and the sajdahs are short.

So this is the opinion about taraweeh, where it comes from. Not the opinion, sorry: the meaning of taraweeh. By the way, it's not the only meaning. Some scholars of the past also said that the term taraweeh comes from the people of Mecca, not Medina: that this tawaf that they would do, they would call that the interlude, and so from the people of Makkah came the taraweeh. And anyway, the point is that both of these terms go back to that rest and interlude, the rest from the long qiyam. So from the long qiyam they would rest by doing tawaf. SubhanAllah, those were the days. We rest by just leaning back and lying down; they would rest by getting invigorated and doing tawaf, subhanAllah.

And one of my teachers, Shaykh Salman al-Awdah, may Allah 'azza wa jall free him from the zulm that he is currently undergoing in jail, Shaykh Salman al-Awdah also said, "I also have a psychological interpretation of taraweeh. It's not historical." He said taraweeh also can come from the phrase *arihna*, *rahah*, which means to find comfort, from the phrase of the Prophet ﷺ, "*Arihna biha ya Bilal*": bring comfort, O Bilal, through the salah. So Shaykh Salman said that the taraweeh is one of the greatest comforts of Ramadan; it brings comfort to our soul, and so it is called taraweeh because we find peace in it. Now, that's not a historical interpretation; it is a psychological one.

Historically speaking, the naming was done in the end of the first or the beginning of the second century, not by the Sahabah, not by the Prophet ﷺ, but by the students of the Sahabah, or maybe even their students, and early scholars. Imam al-Shafi'i and others are using this term taraweeh; no problem over here. Now, Imam al-Shafi'i explicitly said, "I found the people of Medina praying 39, I found the people of Mecca praying 23, and whichever you want to do is fine." And this has been the standard position throughout Islamic history.

Dear Muslims, please do not begin, especially at this time of COVID lockdown, and things are already tense, please do not revert to the very petty issue of 8 versus 20. SubhanAllah, from a historical perspective it is non-existent. This controversy did not exist throughout the ummah. It was begun by one scholar of the last generation, may Allah bless and forgive him, a passionate scholar of hadith, very zealous but very unique in his interpretation, and he began claiming that to pray 20 rak'ah is an innovation, or a bid'ah. And as Shaykh Ibn Uthaymin, my teacher, said, whoever says that to pray more than 8 is a bid'ah, that person himself is saying a bid'ah, because no one before him ever said this in Islamic history. And that is very true.

This interpretation that taraweeh must be a certain number of rak'at is wrong, because taraweeh is not a fard salah. It is a nafil salah. You want to pray more, you want to pray less, you want to pray 20, you want to pray 36, you want to pray whatever: it's not something that Allah 'azza wa jall has legislated. True, our Prophet ﷺ has his own custom and habit. He would pray eight rak'at plus three. Some have added two, which is the introductory: when he would wake up at night, our Prophet ﷺ would pray two very quick rak'ahs, just to begin the qiyam, we should say. This is any day, not just in Ramadan. Then he would pray eight rak'ahs, and Aisha said, don't even ask me how beautiful and long they were. Then he would pray three rak'ahs witr.

But he didn't tell us. In fact, when the companion came and said, "Ya Rasulallah, how do I pray the qiyam al-layl?" he said, "Pray *mathna mathna*. When you think that it's about time to pray Fajr, then stand up and pray witr." So this hadith is explicit. And this has been the position of pretty much the entirety of the ummah for the last 13 and a half centuries, up until one particular shaykh, or 'alim, comes along. And again, may Allah reward and forgive him and bless him for all the good that he has done, but still, everybody is human, and he had a position that went against pretty much everybody else.

And because of this great shaykh, he began a movement that became very popular across the globe, and this movement then began saying to pray eight is the only thing possible; to do more than eight is a bid'ah, or an innovation. And this is, frankly, without any scholarly merit, and I'm being gentle when I say that. There is no scholarly merit in that position whatsoever. This is something that you look at historically.

**Pray whatever you want to pray, but more important than the quantity is the quality.** Please do not discuss back and forth. If somebody says that it is bid'ah to pray 20, jazakAllahu khayr, make sure you pray the 8 as the Prophet ﷺ prayed. End of story. Don't worry about the quantity; worry about the quality more than this.

Now, the point being, therefore: pray as much as you want. It's a nafil salah, or a sunnah salah. Umar ibn al-Khattab clearly instituted 20; whoever wants to pray 20, no problem. And the Prophet ﷺ clearly used to pray 8 plus witr, that's 13; whoever wants to do that, no problem. Please do not make this a point of any animosity. Both positions have historic legitimacy. Even for the one who wants to follow the Prophet's position, more important than the number should be the quality.

And the reason why Umar ibn al-Khattab did 20, remember, was to make it easier. You know, you have a thousand people praying, two thousand people praying; not everybody can spend the entire two hours. People have to leave, people have to come in and out. So when you have shorter rak'at, it makes it easier for the congregation. Therefore both have their positions, and inshaAllah there's no haraj in either one that is done.
